body: The Andøya Rocket Range in northern Norway, several hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, launched its first research rocket in 1962. It was named Ferdinand after the beloved children’s book about a peaceful bull who just wanted to be alone in the field among the flowers and not sent to the bullfights. Since then, more than a thousand research rockets have been launched. In January 1995, one went terribly wrong and almost started World War III. I was a witness, but more on that in a moment. Today, the reports of the activity at Andøya capture the new Cold War in the Arctic. It’s like a snow globe, serene until you shake it—then there’s a storm.

Just before President Donald Trump took office for the second time in January, the US signed a Technology Safeguard Agreement to authorize the transfer of US commercial missile launchers to Norway. Now, Andøya Rocket Range has been rechristened as the Andøya Space Port, as Norway establishes a base for long-range military drones; Norway and the US are building an arctic satellite station to detect incoming enemy missiles. It is the first of its kind outside the United States, according to the Norwegian Minister of Defense, Bjørn Arild Gram. “Space activity is becoming more important for defense cooperation, and Andøya is of great value for Norway as well as for our allies,” said Gram. Map of Norway and Russia Forgotten history Norway, a founding member of NATO, borders Russia on the Barents Sea in the Arctic Ocean. A look at the map will show the City of Murmansk, Russia’s only ice-free port and sole access to the Atlantic Ocean.

The social media photos from Murmansk show grieving mothers clutching flowers in front of fresh graves at new cemeteries full of the area’s sons killed by the fighting in Ukraine. Based on American technology, a Norwegian mobile air defense system is being tested at the new Andøya base for long-range drones. This is a variant of the surface-to-air system that shoots down the Russian drones attacking Kyiv. The Russian invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent threats of the use of nuclear weapons by President Putin has brought Norway back to Viking mode.

All of this is in reaction to Russia building up its nuclear submarine fleet and provocative nuclear war exercises by its navy near Norway. Adding to the risk of conflict is the recent malicious damage to undersea cables in Norwegian waters, including the main communication link to Evenes airbase in north Norway, NATO’s first line of defense nearest Russia.

Alas, the Russians have now ended cooperation on the safekeeping of nuclear weapons and waste relating to the Russian Navy based in Murmansk in place since 1997. I had a hand in negotiating the original agreement and made many trips to Murmansk. On each trip, I passed by the Valley of Glory, where thousands of Soviet (and German) troops died over the five-year battle to prevent Adolf Hitler from taking the port of Murmansk. The Soviet Red Army liberated northern Norway from the German occupation. After the war, the Soviets left, went home, and closed the border again. Only in the early 1990s—after the dissolution of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War—did a new border crossing open. It was a symbol of the optimistic years of the 20th century for America and Europe. Ferdinand the bull could be found again in his field of flowers. But memories are short, and things fell apart again in the Arctic after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Norwegian health authorities sent stockpiles of iodine pills to all parts of the country to be taken in case of radioactive fallout from a nuclear weapons accident. Iodine tablets block the absorption of radioactive material by the thyroid gland and reduce the risk of contracting cancer.

Amid all this reckless Russian saber-rattling, we can count on the Norwegians to do the right thing. They have dealt with the Russians on their border for a thousand years. But it all can go wrong, just by accident. I spent January 18-20, 1995, at the Andøya Rocket Range to witness the launch of an American research rocket. The launch was of the powerful Black Brant XII, which would peak at 1,400 kilometers over the Norwegian island of Svalbard. It was part of a research project by Cornell University to gather daytime data on the northern lights. They had obtained the US rocket under a NASA program. Bad weather at the Range delayed the launch, and I returned to Oslo for meetings with the departing Russian Ambassador. On January 25, the launch went off—and within seconds, the Russian early warning radar system near Murmansk tagged it as a possible nuclear missile attack by the United States. This rocket's speed and suspicious trajectory triggered a mid-level automated alert, and the first steps of the Russian response began. The missile stayed on its course, with the last stage dropping into the sea 320 kilometers northeast of Svalbard. It did not enter Russian airspace, and the alert was over before the Russian general in charge could get from his nearby office to the command-and-control center. Word of this alert reached the Russian news service Interfax. It was first reported that a rocket had been shot down. This was quickly corrected, but the next day, Russian President Boris Yeltsin was quoted as saying he had been given the “black box,” the instrument with the keys to launch a nuclear counterattack. The Russian economy and government were in shambles at this time, and there were domestic political reasons for the mercurial president to appear strong and in charge. Within two days, the world press treated the incident as a farce and an example of Russian incompetence. It was not a joke, and we are all lucky. A lot could have ended in tragedy. Fortunately, the Black Brant remained on course and did not enter Russian airspace, and the Russian early warning system and those in control of it that day acted appropriately. Had the missile been perceived as a threatening nuclear missile, the outcome could have been disastrous. On January 26, the day after the incident, I was with the Russian ambassador for his farewell reception. I certainly did not mention to him (and saw no reason to report to the State Department) that I had been at Andøya just before this launch. We said goodbye and wished each other good luck and, with a full-throated “Nostrovia!” (“Cheers!”) threw down a shot of vodka. It’s time to stop this cat-and-mouse game in which both sides think they are the cat.
Both sides believe the potential for an accidental nuclear incident is high
—obviously, Norway’s Prime Minister thinks so. It’s important to recognize the essential role of diplomacy and cooperation with our allies—and even our enemies—when it comes to nuclear security.
We need to learn from the past, and the US needs to again take a leadership role in avoiding nuclear annihilation

. As former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said: “When we're trying to solve difficult national issues, it's sometimes necessary to talk to adversaries as well as friends. Historians have a word for this: diplomacy.”
